findings.evidence: Pass `"$branch"` quoted. Single quotes are needed only for a literal name you type containing `$` (`'feature/weird$name'`), which the shell would otherwise expand.
findings.fix: Cut this to one clause or delete it. The model already knows how shell quoting works, and step 5 already quotes "$branch".

findings.evidence: If `$remote` is set and `git merge-base --is-ancestor "$remote" "$orig"` fails, the remote has commits the local branch lacks: stop
findings.fix: Add one decision check before any mutation: 'Before rebasing, ask whether anyone else pushes to this branch. If `git log --format=%ae "origin/$target..$remote"` shows authors other than the user, stop.' The description excludes shared branches, but the body never tells the agent how to spot one. Right now it only notices a shared branch when the remote has diverged.

findings.evidence: ## Gotchas lists three items, one of which (line 25) is generic shell quoting
findings.fix: Replace the quoting item with a gotcha from real use, for example: 'Stacked branches: rebasing a branch that other local branches build on leaves them on the old SHAs. Pass `--update-refs` (git 2.38+) or tell the user which dependent branches need rebasing.'

findings.evidence: If the lease is rejected, someone else pushed: stop, do not retry with `--force`.
findings.fix: Finish the lease-rejected branch: 'Report that the local branch is already rebased and was not pushed. Give the pre-rebase tip `$orig` and the recovery command `git reset --hard $orig`. Then list the new remote commits with `git fetch origin && git log --oneline "$branch..origin/$branch"`.' The agent should not leave the user with no next step.

findings.evidence: "If `old_base` is empty, use `fork=$(git merge-base --fork-point "origin/$target" "$branch")`" restricts fork-point discovery to a missing tracking ref. If an IDE or user already fetched an upstream force-push before invocation, `old_base` equals the rewritten tip and its ancestry check passes. The command therefore selects normal explicit-upstream rebase, which defaults to no fork-point detection and can replay retired upstream commits alongside feature commits despite a usable reflog fork point.
findings.fix: Compute the reflog fork point even when `old_base` is set, before selecting normal rebase. When it is non-empty and differs from the ordinary merge base, use `git rebase --onto "origin/$target" "$fork" "$branch"`. Retain the pre-fetch-base fallback for rewrites detected during this fetch; stop for clarification if a known rewrite has no trustworthy cutoff.

findings.evidence: Invoked as `/explain-changes-mental-model` (project install) or `/command-explain-changes-mental-model:explain-changes-mental-model` (this repository's plugin).
findings.fix: Delete the invocation sentence. The harness already handles slash-command discovery and naming, and the model never needs this to do the task. Keep the usage block only if it shows how arguments are classified.
Trim the usage block to the cases section 1 does not already make clear (`HEAD~3` as one commit, `#123`). Every other example repeats a numbered rule in section 1.

findings.evidence: Group files by purpose (not by directory), one group per reviewable idea.
findings.fix: Add a self-check before the output step: 'Before writing the report, compare the groups against `git diff --stat` (or the patch's file list). Every changed file appears in exactly one group, and every Depends on names a group that comes earlier in the review order. Fix the grouping and check again until both hold.' This turns the Process pattern into a checkpointed workflow.

Add a gotcha: '`git diff A..B` is the same as `git diff A B`, not log-range semantics. It includes changes made on A since the branches split, and those appear as reversed hunks. If the user means the changes on the branch only, use `A...B` and say which form you used.' Models routinely assume `..` in diff means what it means in `git log`.
argument-hint: [commit|branch|range|#PR|custom] (the hint is shown at invocation; without it users cannot see that the command supports the PR path in step 4)

findings.evidence: base is the first that exists of `main`, `master`, `origin/main`, `origin/master`, else ask the user for a base; then `git diff "<base>...<arg>" --no-color`.
findings.fix: Handle the branch that resolves to the base and the remote branch. If <arg> is itself the chosen base (for example `/explain-changes-mental-model main`), `main...main` is empty and the command wrongly reports 'No changes found'. In that case explain the tip commit as in step 7, or ask for a base. For a `refs/remotes/<arg>` branch, prefer the matching remote base (`origin/main`), because local `main` may be stale.

findings.evidence: The 28-line Output section includes familiar reporting scaffolding: '### High-Level Summary', '[2-3 sentences: goal and approach]', '**Why this matters:** [context]' and '**Key changes:** [change and why]'. Unlike the expert source-selection, grouping and Gotchas sections, much of this section activates ordinary reporting behavior rather than adding knowledge.
findings.fix: Condense the generic summary, concepts and explanatory fields into a short output instruction. Retain the distinctive requirements: dependency-ordered groups, file references, concrete dependency evidence, enables relationships, review sequence and the single-group exception.

findings.evidence: 'only a successful empty output is an empty diff' does not resolve the verified empty-commit branch: line 30 uses 'git show "<arg>" --no-color', which prints commit metadata even when the commit contains no patch. The command therefore misses its stated no-changes stopping condition for an empty commit.
findings.fix: For non-merge commits and tags, obtain patch-only output with `git show --format= --no-color "<arg>^{commit}"`, fetching metadata separately if needed. Preserve the first-parent diff for merges, and apply the no-changes stopping condition to patch content rather than metadata-bearing stdout.
